text:
emotional regulation is not what I thought it was and I wasted years getting it wrong

For the longest time I thought being emotionally regulated meant keeping your cool. Staying calm. Not overreacting. Basically just... being less emotional.

Turns out that's emotional *suppression* and it's actually worse for you than just losing your shit.

I started reading about this after a therapist told me I was "well-regulated" and I was like... I literally just push everything down? That's good?

She said no. That's the opposite.

Actual emotional regulation (from the research, DERS scale stuff if anyone's curious) has two parts:

**Understanding.** Can you identify what you're actually feeling and why? Not "I'm fine" or "I'm upset" but specifically what's going on. There's a huge difference between feeling rejected, feeling disrespected, and feeling scared, but they can all look like anger on the outside.

**Managing.** Once you know what you're feeling, can you choose how to respond to it instead of just reacting? Not suppressing it. Not exploding. Actually sitting with it long enough to pick a response.

The part that messed me up for years: I was great at managing (read: suppressing) and terrible at understanding. I could keep a straight face in any argument but I had no idea what I was actually feeling until like 3 days later when it would hit me in the shower.

And apparently that's super common, especially for guys who were taught that emotions = weakness. You develop one half of the skill (keep it together) without the other half (know what's happening inside).

The thing that helped me most was absurdly simple. When I notice I'm reacting to something, getting defensive, shutting down, wanting to leave the room, I just ask myself "what am I actually feeling right now, specifically?" Usually the first answer is wrong. "I'm annoyed." Ok but under that. "I feel like she doesn't respect my time." Under that. "I'm scared I don't matter to her." Oh. There it is.

Sounds cheesy but it honestly changed a lot for me. Relationships, work, everything.

Anyone else go through this? Where you thought you were emotionally regulated but you were actually just numb?

**TL;DR:** Emotional regulation isn't staying calm, that's suppression. Real regulation is understanding what you feel (specifically) and choosing how to respond. I spent years confusing the two and it cost me relationships.

text:
How I overcame my phone addiction and changed my life completely.

For YEARS, I felt tired... unmotivated... and stuck with this eternal brain fog. I struggled to get out of bed, stay fit and felt that I was someone who didn't have much potential. I even thought that I was someone who had ADHD and tried meds, self help books, therapy but they never made a lasting difference.

That was until I listened to this episode from Huberman’s podcast on dopamine. I finally understood that my habits, especially those that spiked my dopamine levels were the problem.

He explained how it gives my brain quick and easy artificial 'highs' so it had no reason to work harder for more meaningful ones. That clicked with me. And the biggest culprit was obvious. **My phone.** Where those hours of mindless scrolling were frying my dopamine receptors. By scrolling I was rewarding myself BEFORE doing hard things instead of after, so of course I had no motivation to do anything.

So I made it my mission to change and reduced my screen time from over 10 hours a day to just two.

The result was unbelievable. I woke up with actual energy and stopped procrastinating. My attention span went from goldfish-level to actually functional. When your brain isn't constantly seeking the next hit, it's easier to just do the thing in front of you. And for the first time, I went out of my way to study, workout and bond with family / friends.

A few things that really helped me:

**I stopped using my phone at the gym, on public transport, or during meals.** By sitting with boredom I trained my brain to be comfortable without constant hits of stimulation.

**I set a screentime goal everyday** and tracked it with simple wall calendar. Every morning I put a big 'X' if I was under the goal. Seeing the chain of X's was so satisfying and became a visual proof of progress for me.

**I made it very hard to use addicting apps.** I use an app called Breaktime App Blocker to block my TikTok and Instagram 24/7. Every time I open it, it makes me wait 30 seconds first and most times I put the phone back down. If not, it makes me set a time limit and reblocks it after to hold me accountable. Theres a lot out there so find one that works for you.

**Kept my mornings phone free.** I put my phone in a room, drawer or I literally put it in a tissue box and throw it across the room before bed. This was so important to stop me from burning all my motivation for the day.

**I used other feel good activities as a replacement:** a walk, gyming, cooking, reading, sport, meeting friends and surprisingly chewing gum. When I get that craving to scroll, I pick one of these things and it gives me the same 'happy' feeling that scrolling would've and makes me forget about it.

It's not an easy journey but I wanted to share some tips and just how big of an impact its had. If there's something that worked for you please share below!

I tracked every habit for 365 days. Here's the brutally honest data on what actually changed my life.

Last year I decided to run an experiment on myself. I tracked 12 different habits every single day for a full year using a simple spreadsheet. Wake-up time, exercise, reading, meditation, cold showers, journaling, no alcohol, 8 hours sleep, healthy eating, screen time limits, gratitude practice, and deep work blocks.

Here's what I found after 365 days of data:

The habits that actually moved the needle were embarrassingly simple. Sleep and exercise. That's it. Everything else was noise.

When I slept 7.5+ hours, my productivity the next day was on average 40% higher. When I exercised in the morning, I was 3x more likely to stick to every other habit that day.

Cold showers? Made zero measurable difference after the initial novelty wore off. Meditation? Helpful but only when done consistently for 30+ days straight. Journaling? Great for clarity but didn't move any other metric.

The biggest lesson: stop trying to build 10 habits at once. Lock in sleep and movement first. Everything else becomes dramatically easier after that.

I also noticed a pattern I call the "domino effect" - when I nailed my morning workout, I naturally ate better, focused longer, and went to bed on time. One keystone habit triggered everything else.

If you're feeling overwhelmed trying to change everything at once, just pick ONE thing. For me it was a 30-minute morning walk. That single habit was the domino that knocked everything else into place.

What's your keystone habit? I'm curious if others have noticed similar patterns.

>Before you eat, even if you’re very hungry, just touch the plate and sit there looking at the food for 3 minutes. If you can put off what you really want by just 3 minutes, you’ll become conscious

It sounded simple .... almost too simple. But I decided to try it, not to control cravings, but just out of curiosity.

At first, it felt strange. Sitting in front of food without eating for three minutes felt like an eternity. My mind kept pushing me to start right away. But I stayed with it.

After a few days, I noticed something unexpected. On the days I waited before eating, I felt calmer and more in control and oddly, the usual post-meal sweet craving didn’t hit as hard. I ate what I needed, and that was enough.  
But on the days I forgot to pause, the old craving pattern returned.

That’s when it clicked ....maybe the issue wasn’t the sugar itself, but the unconscious rush to eat. That small three-minute gap created a little space between the urge and the action.

If you also find yourself struggling with cravings or impulsive eating, try this simple 3-minute pause before your meal. It might surprise you how much difference such a tiny shift can make.

text:
The boring middle is where every habit dies and I think I finally figured out why

I have started 14 different "this is the year I change" attempts in the last three years. 

Gym daily, sleeping on time, no weed, journaling, cold showers, you name it. Pick one, I have tried it.

Almost all of them died at the exact same point. Somewhere between week 2 and week 4.

Not week 1. Week 1 is easy. You are high on the idea of yourself. You are not running on discipline, you are running on the chemistry of starting. The new gym, the new routine, the new identity, all of it is dopamine. You confuse this feeling for transformation. It is not. It is novelty.

Not month 6 either. If you make it that far, the thing has basically become you.

The middle. The boring middle. That is where it dies. The part where the novelty has dried up but the new behavior has not become the new identity yet. The part where motivation is gone and discipline has not kicked in either. You feel flat. You think it is not working. You quit. Then you mistake the quitting for proof that you are undisciplined.

Here is what is actually happening, because I read enough dopamine literature this year to finally make sense of why this kept happening to me specifically, and I think it's working for me now.

Days 1 to 7. Dopamine is firing because everything is novel. The reward signal is independent of the behavior itself. You feel powerful. You make plans for who you will be in 6 months. You tell people about your new system. This is the dangerous part, not the good part. You are spending future-you's energy on present-you's vision.

Days 7 to 21. Novelty fades. Dopamine returns to baseline. The behavior now has to compete with every other source of dopamine in your environment. Phone, food, scrolling, weed, whatever your default is. And the brain has not yet built the deeper, slower reward system that comes from sustained behavior. There is a gap. A trough. You feel like the thing has stopped working. It has not stopped working. You have just stopped getting paid in the currency you were getting paid in before.

Days 21 plus. If you survive the trough, the slower system starts kicking in. The behavior starts feeling good in itself, not because of novelty. This is where it actually becomes a habit.

Most people quit during the gap. I have quit during the gap maybe 12 times.

What finally helped me push through it on the attempt I am currently on, day 23 by the way, not day 50, I have not earned the right to claim victory:

Lower the bar in the middle. Whatever your current standard is, cut it by 50 percent during weeks 3 to 5. The goal during the trough is not progress, it is preservation. A 15 minute workout 4 days a week beats a 60 minute workout you skip after week 3. You are not training the behavior in this window. You are training the identity. The identity needs you to show up. It does not care how hard.

Stop romanticizing restarts. Every restart is a small admission that you needed novelty to feel motivated. Continuity through the trough is the actual skill. It is also the only one that compounds. "I will start again on May 1st" is the same dopamine hit as "I will start tomorrow," just dressed up in better clothes.

Pre-commit before you hit the cliff. If you know the trough is coming around day 21, plan for it now. Not the day of. The week before. A smaller version of the habit, ready to go, no decisions required during the trough itself. Decision fatigue is highest exactly when willpower is lowest.

Track the trough specifically. Not your wins. Not your streaks. Track the days you almost quit and what made you not quit. That data is the actual playbook.

Replace "did I do it perfectly today" with "did I show up at all today." Showing up at 30 percent strength builds the identity. Skipping resets it. There is no middle ground here. You are either someone who shows up or someone who does not.

The thing nobody tells you is this. The boring middle is not the obstacle to the habit. The boring middle is the habit. The skill you are actually building is not the behavior itself, it is the ability to keep going when nothing in your nervous system is rewarding you for it. Once you internalize that, the relationship to motivation completely changes. You stop waiting to feel like doing the thing, because you finally understand that not feeling like it is the signal that the rewiring is working.

Anyway. That is the lesson. If anyone is in week 4 right now and reading this thinking it is over, it is not over. You are just in the part nobody warned you about.
label: actionable_advice

Around midnight the guilt would hit and I would start planning a brand new version of myself in my notes app. New morning routine, gym, cooking, reading, side project, all of it. Then the next day I would follow exactly zero of it.

In my head I had two versions of myself. Current me, who is always exhausted and "deserves a break", and future me, who will somehow wake up one magical Monday and be disciplined, organized and productive. I kept waiting for that motivated future me to appear. Spoiler: they never did.

Ten days ago something snapped in a very boring way. No big breakdown, no inspirational quote. I just looked at my list and thought: if I cannot do all of this, can I do one thing that even lazy, tired me would accept.

So I made a rule that felt almost stupidly small. At 10 30 PM, no matter what, WiFi on my phone goes off and I put it in the kitchen. No "one more video", no doomscrolling in bed. I did not touch my diet, workouts, anything else. Just that one rule.

I used it to do 5 minutes of stretching and write down three tasks for the day. That was it.

Now it is day 10. I have gone to bed on time ten nights in a row, done my tiny morning list eight times, and my mood is noticeably less horrible. It scares me a bit that one small boundary did more for me than months of trying to redesign my whole life in one shot.

My question for this sub: how do you keep this going without turning it into another perfection trap. I feel the urge to add five more habits at once because I am finally doing "well". text:
Stop calling yourself lazy. 2025 was the year I realized procrastination is an anxiety problem, not a discipline one.

I’ve spent most of my adult life beating myself up for being "lazy."

I had the goals. I had the to-do lists. I had the time. But when it came down to the one task that actually mattered, I’d suddenly find myself reorganizing my desktop files or deep-cleaning the kitchen. Then I’d spend the rest of the night in a shame spiral, wondering why I couldn't just *be disciplined.*

But this year, something clicked. I realized I wasn’t actually allergic to work. Once I finally started a task, I was usually fine, and sometimes I even enjoyed it.

**The problem wasn't the task. It was how I felt about the task.**

I wasn't avoiding work; I was avoiding the fear of failing, the dread of it not being perfect, or the shame of having put it off for three weeks already. My brain wasn't being lazy. It was just trying to protect me from discomfort.

A few things that actually changed the game for me:

* **Action creates motivation, not the other way around.** Waiting to "feel like it" is a trap. I started forcing myself to just do two minutes. Usually, the motivation showed up at minute three.
* **Shame is a productivity killer.** I thought yelling at myself would make me work harder. It just made my brain associate work with "threat." Replacing "What is wrong with you?" with "Okay, you’re overwhelmed, let’s just do one small thing" changed everything.
* **Managing energy, not time.** No planner can fix burnout or anxiety. I started matching tasks to my mood. If I'm anxious, I do tiny wins. If I'm calm, I do the deep work.

It turned out I didn’t need a better planner. I just needed to stop treating myself like a broken machine. I actually ended up creating a simple tracking system around this for myself to handle the mood check-ins and the task matching. It’s been surprisingly helpful for keeping me unstuck, especially on the days when my brain just wants to shut down.

If you’ve been calling yourself lazy for years, I promise you: you’re probably just overwhelmed or scared. You don’t have to fight your brain. You can actually work with it.

If anyone else is dealing with this, I’d love to hear how you handle that "paralysis" feeling.

The habit that fixed my other habits (not what I expected)

39, two kids, five part-time jobs. For years I tried to brute-force discipline. Wake at 5am. Gym daily. No alcohol. Track everything.

It worked in bursts. Then it collapsed. Then guilt. Then another attempt.

What finally broke the cycle was adding one thing: three written questions every morning. Not goals. Not affirmations. Just questions like:

* "What am I avoiding today?"
* "Where am I confusing motion with progress?"
* "What would I do if I stopped trying to prove something?"

Answering in writing: before coffee, before the day starts, this became the anchor that held everything else in place.

Why it works (I think):

The gym isn't the keystone habit. The journal is. If I write in the morning, I go to the gym. If I go to the gym, I don't drink. If I don't drink, I sleep well. If I sleep well, I write the next morning.

Miss the journal? The whole chain wobbles.

I'm on day 300+. Not perfect—I've had weeks where I skipped the gym, weeks where I drank. But I've only missed maybe 10 journal days total. That's the gateway.

text:
Motivation is temporary, discipline is doing the thing regardless of how you feel

I spent years waiting for motivation to show up. Thought one day I'd wake up and finally feel like doing the things I needed to do. Spoiler: that never happened.

Motivation is just a temporary emotion. It comes and goes. You can't build a life around waiting to feel motivated because you'll be waiting forever.

I finally started doing things while completely unmotivated. No energy, no desire, just going through the motions because they needed to get done. And that's when I realized discipline isn't about feeling like doing something. It's about choosing to do it anyway.

Discipline is acting despite the lack of desire, not because of it. It's getting up and going to the gym when every part of you wants to stay in bed. It's working on your project when you'd rather scroll your phone. It's doing the hard thing when doing nothing would be so much easier.

But here's what I'm struggling with: how do you actually build that discipline when every fiber of your being resists? When the gap between what you should do and what you want to do feels impossible to bridge?

I know the answer is supposed to be "just do it anyway" but there's got to be more to it than that. Some days I can push through. Other days the resistance wins and I accomplish nothing.

Like yesterday I had a whole list of things to do, ended up playing jackpot city for two hours instead, felt terrible about it, but still couldn't make myself start the actual work.

How do you train yourself to consistently act against your own feelings? How do you build the muscle of doing things you don't want to do when your default mode is avoidance?

I've made some progress but it still feels like I'm fighting myself constantly. Is that just what discipline is? An endless internal battle? Or does it eventually get easier?

I stopped relying on motivation and made journaling a three question appointment

For years I treated journaling like a mood. If I felt reflective, I wrote. If not, the notebook stayed shut, and every restart felt heavier than the last.

What worked was treating it like an appointment I keep with myself. Every night at the same time I answer the same three questions, and I am done in about five minutes.

What did I do today that is worth remembering?
What is one thing that went better than expected?
What is the one thing I want to get right tomorrow?

The rules matter more than the questions. I never skip twice in a row. I never edit what I wrote. And I keep the streak visible, because watching a quiet little chain grow turned out to be stronger than any burst of motivation.

[Story] I noticed I kept making simple tasks take longer because I wanted to finish them in a way I wouldn't have to revisit

I realized I was spending more time trying to make tasks impossible to regret than actually getting them done.

It showed up in stupidly small ways. I'd spend 40 minutes writing an email that needed maybe five. I'd reorganize a folder before putting a file in it. I'd reread something I'd already understood because I wanted to be absolutely sure I hadn't missed anything.

None of these things looked like procrastination. I was sitting at my desk, paying attention, doing work. If someone had walked past, I'd have looked pretty productive.

The weird part was that I wasn't necessarily afraid of doing the task badly. I was trying to avoid having to come back to it.

I wanted the email to need no clarification. The file to never need moving again. The decision to remain correct after I learned something new. I was treating every ordinary task like it should be a one-time event with no maintenance afterward.

I started noticing how often this made my days worse. A five-minute task would become a little project, and then I'd feel behind, which made me rush the next thing, which gave me another thing to revisit later.

One afternoon, I caught myself changing a perfectly understandable sentence for the fourth time. I wasn't improving its meaning anymore. I was just trying to eliminate the possibility that someone might misunderstand it.

So I tried a couple of small rules:

\- For routine tasks, I decide what finished looks like before starting. For that email, it was simply: the question is clear, the necessary information is included, and there are no obvious mistakes.

\- If I'm revisiting something, I have to name what new information I'm using to justify the revision. If the answer is just 'I want to check once more,' I leave it alone unless there's a real consequence to being wrong.

\- I keep a short list of things I'm allowed to fix later instead of trying to anticipate every possible future problem now.

What surprised me was that I didn't suddenly become careless. I still corrected genuine mistakes. I just stopped spending equal effort on things that had wildly different consequences.

The counterintuitive part is that I used to think discipline meant taking every task seriously. Now I'm starting to think part of being disciplined is knowing which tasks don't deserve that much seriousness in the first place.

I'm still figuring this out, especially with work where mistakes actually matter. I don't want to replace overthinking with rushing, and sometimes that extra check really is worthwhile.

But I can see how often I used thoroughness as an excuse to avoid the uncomfortable feeling of letting something be done without knowing exactly how it would turn out.

Does anyone else struggle with this particular kind of overdoing things? How do you tell the difference between genuinely being thorough and just trying to make a task impossible to regret?

For context, I've been spending around \*\*30–40 hours every week on Instagram Reels\*\*. That's an insane amount of time when I look at it objectively, but it somehow became a normal part of my routine. Whenever I felt bored, tired, uncomfortable, or just didn't feel like studying, I'd open Instagram and start scrolling. Before I knew it, hours had passed.



Today, I finally deactivated my Instagram account. I'm pretty confident that I won't reactivate it, and I genuinely want to change my habits this time. I've also had YouTube Shorts blocked for about a year, so I thought removing Instagram would make a significant difference.



But here's the problem: \*\*even after removing Instagram, I'm still wasting time.\*\*

Instead of scrolling Reels, I now find myself watching long-form YouTube videos, doing random things on my laptop, or finding other activities to occupy my time. Sometimes I don't even have a particular thing I want to watch or do. I just keep finding ways to avoid studying.

It's almost as if I've removed one distraction only to replace it with another.



\## My situation right now

I'm preparing for UCEED, and I have approximately three months left to prepare for the exam. Getting into a good college is genuinely important to me, and I want to give myself the best possible chance.

My current mock scores are around \*\*110–120 out of 300\*\*, while I need approximately 200+ to have a realistic shot at my target campus. I know that's a significant improvement to make in a relatively short period, which is precisely why I can't afford to keep wasting so much time.

Ideally, I need to put in around \*\*6–8 hours of focused study every day\*\* for the next three months. I'm not expecting to become some productivity machine overnight, but I need to become consistent enough to give myself a fighting chance.

The frustrating part is that I understand what I need to do. I have a clear goal, I know how important these next few months are, and I know that spending hours watching videos isn't going to help me get into my target college.

Yet, knowing all of that doesn't seem to translate into action.



\## The cycle I keep getting stuck in

My biggest problem isn't necessarily that I never study. It's that I struggle to maintain the habit.

Sometimes I manage to start studying and have a reasonably productive day. I feel good about myself and think that I've finally got things under control. But after a few hours, I get distracted, lose interest, or start looking for something else to do.

Even when I manage to get into a decent routine, it usually lasts only a few days at most before I fall back into my old habits.

Then I start wasting time again, feel guilty about losing another day, remind myself how little time I have left, and promise myself that I'll study seriously from tomorrow.

And then the same thing happens again.

The closer the exam gets, the more pressure I feel. But instead of that pressure making me work harder, I sometimes end up avoiding the very thing I'm worried about.

I think part of the problem is that studying requires sustained effort, whereas watching videos gives me something entertaining without requiring much effort. Even when I'm aware that I should be studying, I find myself choosing the easier option.

I don't know whether this is a problem with my attention span, my habits, my ability to tolerate boredom, my study methods, or some combination of these things.



I'm not trying to diagnose myself or blame everything on dopamine. I just know that my current behaviour isn't working, and I need to change it.

\## Why I'm worried

Three months might sound like enough time, but when I look at my current scores and the improvement I need, I realise that every week matters.



I don't want to reach the end of these three months knowing that I had enough time to improve but spent most of it procrastinating.

At the same time, I don't want to make another unrealistic plan where I suddenly decide to study for eight hours every day, follow it for two days, burn out, and return to square one.

text:
Why is it so easy to plan your life but so hard to actually follow through?

You make a plan. You tell yourself that tomorrow you'll wake up earlier, study, work out, stop wasting time on your phone, and finally get your life together.

Then tomorrow comes, and somehow you're back to your old habits.

I think one of the biggest problems with self-improvement is that planning feels like progress. You get the satisfaction of imagining a better version of yourself without having to do any of the actual work.

And when you inevitably fail to follow your perfect routine, you feel like you lack discipline. So you make an even better plan and try again.

Maybe the solution isn't finding a better routine. Maybe it's making the routine so small that you can follow it even on a bad day.

Instead of planning to study for three hours, start with 15 minutes. Instead of trying to eliminate every distraction, put your phone in another room for one session.

Not because small actions will magically transform your life overnight, but because consistently doing something is more useful than repeatedly planning to do everything.

I'm curious: what's the biggest reason you struggle to follow through on your plans — unrealistic expectations, distractions, lack of motivation, or something else?

GENERAL ADVICE: You're not stuck because you lack potential. You're stuck because you refuse to face reality.

One of the most important things you can do for yourself is learn to see your life as it actually is, not as you wish it were.  
Spend time with people who are ahead of you. Spend time with people at your level. Observe where you stand, what you’re lacking, and what you need to improve. Don’t avoid situations that make you uncomfortable just because they expose the gap between where you are and where you want to be.  
There’s nothing wrong with having high ambitions or believing in your potential. But potential means very little if you’re not doing anything to realise it.  
Convincing yourself that everything is fine when you know you’re falling behind doesn’t protect you. It just makes it easier to stay where you are.  
**Real growth begins when you stop protecting your ego from reality and start using that reality to improve.**  
Be honest about where you stand, don’t give up on where you want to be, and do the work to close the gap. That’s when things start to change.

text:
Discipline isn’t suffering

Society convinced you that discipline means struggle, it’s not, putting your shoes on going to the gym is not struggling, reading isn’t struggling, learning isn’t struggling, it’s the same thing as you can be cold and wet and miserable or you can just be cold and wet, Discipline is just a term nowadays associated with all these negative emotions of struggle and suffer and punishment, It’s not, It’s simply a bridge to your desires, and it’s easy, The actual tasks are simple and mundane, It’s the psychology war you have inside your mind before, that is what makes it a suffering and a struggle, so eliminate it, I eliminated mine and I’ve been disciplined, 

\- how do you eliminate it? Its a simple concept, For most people discipline is - Decision -> Psychological war -> the actual task, You skip the psychological war part, so it’s just Decision -> The actual task, Dive first thing into the task, you will realize it ain’t hard and it ain’t suffering and it’s actually easy and interesting once you are invested. The more you think about doing something, the harder it becomes, the more you actually do the thing, the mind calibrates itself to the action. Just control your hands and legs, the start the task, don’t listen to your mind, don’t ask for permission, Pretend it doesn’t exist. Thats how you do it. 

\- Now Discipline that feels like punishment, how do you eliminate that? Instead of being 100% disciplined, let’s be 50% disciplined, so throughout your day if you have 6 hours of free time, you can do whatever you want for 3 hours, play video games, eat, watch youtube, etc. and for 3 hours you be productive,   
For example, you come home at work at let’s say 6 pm, you have till 12 pm, that’s 6 hours. Here’s how I do it -   
6 pm - 7:30 pm - Chill  
7:30 pm - 9 pm - Productive  
9 pm - 10:30 pm - Eat and chill  
10:30 pm - 12 pm - productive

Boom, that’s 3 hours of productivity right there, and I do this everyday. On weekends you can stretch it to 6-7 hours of productivity, It’s an easy system without restrictions.

text:
[Method] 3 small changes that cut my "just checking one thing" scrolling

You pick up your phone to check one thing, and forty minutes later you're still scrolling. It's not a willpower problem. It's how the phone is set up. Three changes that actually stuck for me:

1. Put it out of reach.

If it's in your hand, you'll use it. Charge it in another room at night, or keep it in a drawer while you study or work. A few extra steps is enough friction to break the automatic grab. (There's research suggesting a phone just being nearby pulls on your attention, even face-down.)

2. Make it boring.

Turn off every notification you don't actually need, and move your favourite apps off the home screen into a folder. No buzz, no bright icons, much less pull. Greyscale mode helps too, if you can stand it.

3. Have a better swap ready.

The urge doesn't disappear, so give it somewhere to go. Keep a book on your pillow and a ball or your shoes by the door. When you reach for your phone, something better is already waiting.

The big one for me was #1. Out of sight really did mean out of mind after a week.

What's worked for you? I'm collecting ideas.

text:
I realized I was saying “just a minute” way too often

I've been thinking about a small thing lately.

How many times have we told someone, “Just a minute, let me finish this,” while looking at our phones?

One more reel. One more comment. One more thing to check.

And the weird part is that the person sitting next to us usually doesn't argue. They just wait.

My wife used to ask me to put my phone away when we were watching a movie or having dinner. I'd put it away, of course. But the habit would come back whenever she wasn't around to remind me.

I tried app blockers and screen-time limits, but I could always work around them.

It made me wonder: why do most solutions make us feel guilty about using our phones instead of reminding us what we're missing?

That conversation with my wife eventually led me to build **KinMode**.

The idea is simple. When you reach for a distracting app during family time, instead of seeing the same boring “App Blocked” message, you can see a personal reminder from someone you love.

It might say, “Honey, the movie's not the same without you.” Or “Hubby, dinner's getting cold ❤️” Or, when it's bedtime, “Daddy, come tuck me in!”

And the reminders can keep changing, with different messages and the little names your loved ones actually call you, so it doesn't feel like you're seeing the same robotic warning every time.

I liked the thought that a phone could remind you of the people waiting for you, rather than just telling you what you're not allowed to open.

I'm not saying phones are evil or that we should never scroll. I enjoy using mine too.

I just don't want the people I love to always get whatever attention is left over.

I'm curious: Would a reminder that sounds like something your partner or child would actually say make you more likely to put your phone down? Or would you just dismiss it and keep scrolling?

Why white noise might be hurting your focus and sleep (and how pink noise works differently)

A lot of people trying to fix their sleep schedule or build a solid deep-work routine turn to background noise machines or 10-hour static loops to block out distractions.

If you have ever tried this and felt oddly fatigued, tense, or woke up feeling unrefreshed, it is not just in your head. It comes down to how your auditory cortex processes different sound frequencies.

Pure white noise contains equal energy across every audible frequency from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Because the human ear is anatomically far more sensitive to higher pitches (around 2,000 to 5,000 Hz), white noise sounds disproportionately sharp and hissy, like television static. For many people, that continuous high-frequency bombardment triggers low-level autonomic arousal rather than calm focus.

Pink noise, on the other hand, reduces power by 3 dB per octave. This produces a "1/f" spectral density that mirrors both human loudness perception and the natural oscillatory rhythms of neural firing.

In sleep and cognitive labs, EEG studies found that listening to pink noise actually synchronizes with slow-wave delta brainwaves during non-REM sleep. Instead of keeping the sensory cortex on alert, it stabilizes neural activity and helps sustain the deep sleep stages responsible for memory consolidation and waking mental clarity.

If pure white noise makes you feel agitated or leaves you feeling fatigued, switching down the spectrum to pink noise (or even deeper brown noise) is usually a night-and-day difference for cognitive stamina.

[Story] I noticed I was avoiding my routine by doing the easy parts of it really well

I realized I could spend an entire evening being productive and still avoid the one thing I had planned to do.

Not by scrolling or watching videos. I'd clean my desk, reply to emails, organize my notes, refill my water bottle, and even prepare everything for the next morning. All perfectly reasonable things to do. The problem was that I'd somehow do all of them before touching the task I'd actually promised myself I'd finish.

Last Tuesday, I spent about 25 minutes reorganizing a folder of study materials. The folder looked great. Everything was labeled, sorted, and easy to find. I felt weirdly satisfied with myself until I noticed I hadn't read a single page of what I was supposed to study.

The embarrassing part is that I wasn't even consciously making excuses. I genuinely felt busy. If someone had asked what I'd been doing, I could have listed six things without admitting that I'd avoided the seventh.

I started noticing this pattern whenever a task had an unclear next step. I'd gravitate toward something nearby that had an obvious finish line. Cleaning has a finish line. Answering an email has a finish line. Learning something difficult usually doesn't give you that same immediate sense of completion.

What surprised me was that trying to become more disciplined sometimes made this worse. I got better at building routines, but I also got better at finding respectable activities to hide inside them.

A few small changes have helped me catch it:

\- Before starting my routine, I write down the specific piece of work that would make the session count. Not 'study,' but something like 'solve the first three problems without looking at the answers.'

\- When I catch myself preparing for more than a few minutes, I leave the setup imperfect and attempt the actual task first. I can organize things afterward if I still need to.

\- At the end of the day, I look at what I actually attempted, not how many useful-looking things I completed. Sometimes the answer is uncomfortable, but at least I know what happened.

Here's the counterintuitive part: I don't think my problem was always procrastination in the usual sense. Sometimes I was working hard to avoid the particular kind of work where effort might not produce a satisfying result immediately.

And I don't want to turn every small task into something suspicious, either. Cleaning, planning, and preparation are genuinely necessary sometimes. The difference seems to be whether they support the difficult task or quietly replace it.

I'm still trying to figure out where that line is, especially on days when I'm tired and doing anything useful feels like a win.

\*\*Do you ever find yourself becoming extremely productive around the task you're avoiding?\*\* What does that look like for you, and how do you tell when preparation has stopped being useful?

[Method] I stopped fighting my worries and started scheduling them. 15 minutes a day.

For years I tried to "just stop overthinking." It never worked. The harder I pushed a thought away, the louder it got.

What finally helped was a simple trick therapists call worry postponement. I call it a worry window:

1. Pick 15 minutes at the same time every day. Mine is 5:30 pm. Not the hour before bed.
2. When a worry shows up outside that time, write it in a phone note and tell yourself "not now, later."
3. Go back to whatever you were doing.
4. At your window, read the list. For each item ask: can I act on this? If yes, plan one small step. If no, let it go or carry it to tomorrow.
5. When the timer ends, stop. Get up and do something with your hands.

The surprising part: by the time the window comes, about half the list doesn't feel important anymore. That taught my brain more than any amount of arguing with it.

If a worry is truly urgent, it isn't a worry, it's a task. Do it now.

Anyone else tried this? What time of day works for you?

text:
The neurological reason you lose all motivation the moment after making an immaculate plan

Ever spend a Sunday evening mapping out a flawless daily routine, study schedule, or project roadmap—feeling an intense rush of energy and excitement—only to wake up the next morning feeling completely numb and exhausted before you even start task one?

It feels like a personal failure of willpower, but cognitive neuroscience calls this "premature reward signaling." 

Pioneering research on goal realization (like Peter Gollwitzer’s studies at NYU) demonstrated that when we meticulously plan and mentally simulate our future accomplishments, our brain’s reward centers (particularly the nucleus accumbens) release a premature burst of dopamine. In essence, the subconscious brain registers the act of planning as actual progress toward the goal.

By the time morning rolls around and you face the actual, friction-filled mechanical effort, the novelty is gone and dopamine levels crater. You’ve already "spent" the neurochemical reward before taking a single physical step.

The fix researchers suggest is shifting from broad outcome planning to rigid "Implementation Intentions" (If/Then triggers) that separate planning from emotional reward, focusing only on the immediate physical action rather than the future identity.

How do you personally handle the gap between planning and execution? Do you find that keeping plans deliberately vague or extremely small helps protect your follow-through?

The 11-Day week

I am proposing a new week, aiming for better recovery and possibly better output                                         

The traditional week cycle has 7 days, unlike the year, which is calculated by completing one revolution around the sun; a month is calculated by a moon's cycle, and a day is Earth completing a rotation on its axis, but the week has no strong relation to an astronomical cycle. The 7-day week also has a background with astrology and outdated astronomical knowledge; the 7-day week is culturally symbolic, but doesnt have a strong rational basis, it is also not necessarily the best fit for our body fatigue recovery and overall reset. Hence, I am proposing the 11-day week.

This structure is supposed to align with recovery patterns, and productivity is not linear to the amount of hours we put in; beyond a point, we get diminishing returns. After 5 -6 days of work, we reach burnout and then get a shorter window of recovery, and also run errands after a longer work week. Instead, we will have the 11-day week structure.

4 days -Work

1 day off

4 days-work

2 days-off

Working hours will be the same, 7-8 hours

With a break in the middle, it helps in short recovery, along with a deep recovery and rest at the end of the week .

This structure will have only 3 weeks per month instead of 4 weeks per month

In a 7-day week, the working days would be 5-6 days with 21-24 working days a month, a11-day week would have similar working days of 22-24 working days a month but more time to rest with around 8- 9 holidays ( one rest day can be optional, but 3 days rest would be recommended), this could improve productivity however AI simiulationan and pilot testing would be required to test this hypothesis.

text:
You can become obsessed with discipline and still avoid changing your life.

There's a strange form of procrastination that looks almost exactly like self-improvement. You wake up and design a better routine, you research habit trackers, watch videos about consistency, read about willpower and reorganize your schedule. By the end of the day, you've spent hours thinking about becoming a different person but the thing you were supposed to do is still untouched. I find this fascinating because the problem isn't necessarily laziness. Sometimes preparing to improve ourselves gives us enough psychological satisfaction that we never reach the uncomfortable part of actually changing. Planning offers clarity, research offers reassurance, a new system offers the excitement of a fresh beginning.

Actual repetition offers very little of that. It's often boring, imperfect and difficult to measure. You don't get to reinvent yourself every morning and you just have to return to the same ordinary actions. It's a paradox I explored in Invisible Discipline: the very systems we create to escape procrastination can sometimes become its most sophisticated form. The difficult question isn't always whether you have enough discipline sometimes it's whether your pursuit of discipline has become the most sophisticated way you've found to procrastinate.

At what point does working on yourself become a way of avoiding the work itself?

text:
I failed at 15 morning routines before discovering this - The 2-minute framework that actually works

Then I studied why 60M people use Duolingo daily but can't stick to morning routines. Found a 4-part framework that works.

My Failed Morning Routines:

1. 60-min morning routine - Lasted 3 days

2. 30-min meditation + gym - Lasted 1 week  

3. 5 AM club - Lasted 2 days, def. not a morning person

4. Miracle morning - Lasted 4 days

5. Journaling every morning - Lasted 5 days

...you get the idea. Total failure rate: 100%

What Finally Worked:

Studied products with 40-60% retention:

\\- Duolingo: 60M daily users

\\- Wordle: 10M daily players

\\- Headspace: 70M users

Found they all use the same 4-part psychology framework.

The Framework:

1. Tiny Time Investment (2-3 min max)

  

Winners:

\\- Duolingo: 3-5 min lessons

\\- Wordle: 2 min puzzle

\\- Headspace: 3-10 min meditation

  

Losers:

\\- "I'll read for 30 min daily" - Lasts 2 days

\\- "I'll journal for 20 min" - Too much friction

  

The magic number: 2-3 minutes. Short enough you can't say "I'm too busy."

  

2. Immediate Reward (Dopamine NOW)

Winners:

\\- Duolingo: Green checkmark + XP instantly

\\- Wordle: Solve animation + share

\\- Strava: Kudos from friends

  

Losers:

\\- I'll work out to get fit - Results take weeks

\\- I'll learn Python to get a job - Delayed gratification

  

You need instant satisfaction, not future promises.

3. Visible Progress (Identity over Goals)

Winners:

\\- Duolingo: 47-day streak visible

\\- Wordle: Share your solve pattern

\\- GitHub: Green commit squares

This shifts identity:

Not "I'm trying to learn Spanish

But "I'm someone with a 47-day streak"

Atomic Habits principle: You become your habits.

  

4. Social Pressure (Optional But 2x Retention)

Winners:

\\- Duolingo: Friend streaks

\\- Strava: Community sees your runs

\\- Apple Watch: Share activity

Knowing someone else sees your progress doubles retention.

  

What I Tested:

Applied this to something nobody's built habits around: PURPOSE.

  

Everyone has:

\\- Body habits (gym)

\\- Mind habits (meditation)

\\- Productivity habits (journaling)

  

Nobody has:

\\- Soul habits (purpose/impact)

  

Built a 2-minute daily ritual:

\\- Learn about someone doing meaningful work (90 sec)

\\- Quick reflection (30 sec)

\\- Build streak

Testing with 10 people. 8 said they'd do it daily.

Why This Framework Works:

Duolingo doesn't make you fluent. It makes you CONSISTENT. The product is the HABIT, not the outcome. Once you have the daily habit, the outcome follows.

The Mistake Most People Make:

They start with the GOAL:

\\- "I want to be fluent in Spanish"

\\- "I want to lose 20 lbs"

\\- "I want to be more productive"

  

They should start with the SYSTEM:

\\- I'll do 3 minutes of Duolingo after coffee

\\- I'll walk 10 minutes after dinner

\\- I'll journal 2 minutes before bed

  

Goals fade. Systems stick.

  

Why My Previous Routines Failed:

Too long (30-60 min) - I'll do it later

Delayed reward ("Get fit in 3 months") - No dopamine

No visible progress - Forgot about it. No accountability

  

What Changed: 

\\- 2 minutes (impossible to skip)   

\\- Immediate reward (feel good NOW)   

\\- Visible streak (accountability)   

\\- Social pressure (optional)   

  

65 days straight now. First routine that's lasted.   

  

Questions for you:   

1. What morning routines have you failed at? Why?   

2. What's the longest you've maintained a daily habit?   

3. Is 2 minutes realistic or too short?   

  

Failed 15 times before getting this right. Happy to share what I learned.

text:
You don't have a discipline problem. I spent 30 years thinking I did.

I know this is a strange thing to say in this sub. Hear me out.

I'm 52. I spent most of my adult life believing that if I just found the right system — the right routine, the right habits, the right structure — everything would click. I optimised my mornings. I tracked my habits. I did the hard things. And for stretches it worked, in the way that anything works when you throw enough willpower at it.

But it never held. And I couldn't figure out why. I thought the problem was me. Not enough consistency. Not enough grit. So I'd find a new system and start again.
It took me an embarrassingly long time to realise the problem was never discipline. It was that I had no idea what I was being disciplined for.

Discipline in service of nothing is just a more respectable way to stay busy. And staying busy is one of the most effective ways men avoid asking themselves what they actually want.

I built a business. It failed — not because I wasn't talented, but because I was disciplined about the wrong things. I was showing up every day for a version of my life that I'd never consciously chosen. And the routine, the structure, the systems — they all helped me avoid noticing that.

Here's what I've learned since:

The men who are actually stuck aren't undisciplined. They're misdirected. They can do hard things. They prove it every day. But they're climbing a ladder that's leaning against the wrong wall, and no amount of habit tracking fixes that.

"I just need to be more consistent" is sometimes a lie you tell yourself so you don't have to face the scarier question: consistent at what, and why? If you can't answer that clearly, more discipline is just more avoidance with better packaging.

The real hard thing isn't the cold shower. It's sitting still long enough to be honest about what you're afraid of. Most men I talk to would rather do an hour of burpees than ten minutes of that. I was the same way for years.

I'm not saying discipline doesn't matter — it does. But it's a tool, not an identity. And if you've been cycling through systems and routines and still feel like something's off, it might not be that you haven't found the right one. It might be that you're asking the wrong question.

I'm not a coach. I don't have a programme or a course. I'm a man who works in consulting, lives in east London, and spent thirty years learning all of this the hard way. These days I have honest conversations with men about the stuff underneath the systems — the direction questions, the identity questions, the "what am I actually building and why" questions. On WhatsApp, for free, no strings.

text:
THE SIX COMPONENTS OF A *WEAK IDENTITY*

A weak identity is predictable. It follows patterns. It collapses under minimal stress. It exaggerates small wins and breaks under pressure. It survives, but it never dominates.

Here are the six traits that give it away:

**1. Borrowed Beliefs**

Nothing in your mind is truly yours.  
You absorbed beliefs from parents, teachers, random people online, old failures, cheap compliments, and bad environments. You have never audited them. You just run them like inherited software.

A weak identity treats every belief as truth and never asks:  
“Did I choose this, or did I absorb it?”

Your beliefs are second-hand.  
Your ambition is third-hand.  
Your self-image is a hand-me-down that never fit.

**2. Negotiable Standards**

A weak identity has “standards” that crumble the moment life becomes inconvenient.

You know the type:

* says *“I’m disciplined”* but caves to the first distraction
* says *“I respect myself”* but accepts trash behavior from others
* says *“I’m serious now”* until it rains, they’re tired, or someone invites them out

Weak identities are built on conditional rules.  
Nothing is enforced. Everything is delayed.  
Discipline only exists in their imagination.

**3. Reactive Behavior Loops**

Most people don’t act. They react.  
They live in emotional autopilot.

• If they feel tired, they stop.  
• If they feel insecure, they quit.  
• If someone judges them, they shrink.  
• If the environment changes, they crumble.

There is no internal engine.  
Only weather.

A weak identity is a puppet pulled by whatever emotion shows up first.  
And puppets never run the show.

**4. Self-Image Anchored to Old Evidence**

You still see yourself as the sum of past failures.  
Old grades, old rejections, old expectations, old environments.

Your self-image is outdated, but you still run life based on an expired profile.

[](https://medium.com/plans?source=upgrade_membership---post_li_non_moc_upsell--5094734dd47c---------------------------------------)

A weak identity is obsessed with:

* the person they used to be
* the mistakes they made
* the limits they once had
* the version of themselves others used to recognize

Self-image becomes a prison built from memories.

**5. Fear-Based Decision Patterns**

Weak identities don’t choose what moves them forward.  
They choose what hurts the least.

Every action is designed to avoid discomfort:

* avoiding rejection
* avoiding effort
* avoiding judgment
* avoiding pressure
* avoiding responsibility

This creates the illusion of “peace.”  
But it’s not peace.  
It’s sedation.

You’re not avoiding pain.  
You’re avoiding growth.

**6. Identity Fragmentation**

You think you have one identity.  
You actually have several conflicting ones.

One version wants to win.  
One version wants to hide.  
One wants discipline.  
One wants comfort.  
One wants respect.  
One wants attention.  
One wants silence.  
One wants validation.  
One wants to disappear.

Weak identities are internal civil wars.  
No single version leads.  
No single version is consistent.  
No single version is strong enough to override the others.

This fragmentation destroys momentum.  
It makes you unpredictable even to yourself.

127 days free from corn addiction. This is how I did it and what I've learned.

I'm not the most disciplined person. I've been trying to quit for about ten years.

I hit 127 days today, and this is what has worked for me.

**1. AIM FOR THE PERSON YOU WANT TO BECOM.** The best version of you, the focused one, the one with drive, the one God is proud of, already exists. However, that ideal you have is buried under layers of sin and other vices. You have so much more potential than you think. Find out who you are and how to reveal it to the world, and this will make it much easier for you to overcome sin and porn addiction specifically. You're not becoming someone. You're being revealed.

**2. WILLPOWER ALONE IS NOT ENOUGH.** Phone charges outside the bedroom. Use blockers if you're ok with that. Delete the social media apps and other time wasters if you don't need it for business. As many of us know, they are the gateway to a relapse. Also, take care of yourself. Every relapse I ever had was decided hours before it happened. I was engaging in fantasies, had been scrolling looking at "safe" pics on social media, etc. Take these as warning signs and immediately resolve the situation.

**3. THE BATTLE IS WAGED IN THE MIND AND SPIRIT.** All relapses begin first in the mind as thoughts. As thoughts they must be dismissed and destroyed and not allowed to inseminate the rest of your mind and world. During inevitable times of temptation, the lustful addictive thoughts will provide you with many reasons to relapse. At this time, if you do not present to them a more powerful army of reasons to NOT relapse, then you will lose that battle. Write down why you're doing this, and what's at stake if you remain addicted. Record yourself reading those out and listen to them during times of crisis, especially at night while trying to sleep. You can also use an app to do this which is what I prefer because the lines are generated for you and so won't get repetitive.

**4. DO NOT JUST SIT THERE AND "FIGHT."** Sitting there resisting is a negotiation, and you're negotiating with a professional demon who knows you intimately. The urge is a wave. It peaks and dies in 15-20 minutes IF you don't feed it. Do not have discussions with it, focus on what's at stake, and why you're doing this instead of trying to negotiate with it.

**5. IF NOT NOW, WHEN?** If you keep doing the same thing you've been doing, why would anything change? If you don't level yourself up, how will you level up your life? A magical moment is not going to come when it automatically and effortlessly comes together. One must take actions and break patterns. Do not leave it for tomorrow, do not put it off. You cannot afford to be addicted or to have your self-confidence as a man be chipped away daily by this addiction or any addiction. This is a matter of survival vs living a glorious and blessed life. Take it serious.

**6. THE MIDDLE IS BRUTAL, EXPECT IT.** After several weeks, the demon will begin to stir. At this point you must meet it with calmness, and if your reasons for doing this and your trust and purpose is set in stone with God, then you will destroy the enemy. However, expect symptoms such as a foggy mind, insomnia, restlessness, and the occasional "what's even the point." This is the crucible all of us must pass through. It's not unique. Follow the example of Christ who dismantled and trampled the serpent in the wilderness.

**8. FILL THE HOLE PORN WILL LEAVE BEHIND.** All that newfound time and energy has to go somewhere. Find your purpose. Find why you are born, and put effort into discovering what future you would need to be building for you to wake up excited to work on it or stay up late when the world is asleep just to work on your thing. Focus on improving yourself, for yourself, family, friends, and allow God to guide you towards becoming someone who will uplift mankind.

**9. A SLIP IS A SLIP, IT IS NOT GAME OVER.** Do not let the serpent whisper to you that "oh, since you messed up, no harm in doing it the entire day." That is complete bullshit. Do not ever give in to the serpent, or to those thoughts of doubt and reckless hedonism if you prefer a more non-religious way to put it. The point is to beat the devil. The point is to command yourself. Do not ever take direction or guidance from the enemy.

Keep going everyone, God bless.

text:
I replaced my phone alarm with spoken Stoic quotes — it actually changed my mornings

For years I was the guy who snoozed 4-5 times every morning. Set three alarms, still late. Tried everything — putting my phone across the room, those apps that make you solve math problems, even a sunrise lamp. Nothing stuck longer than a week.

A few months ago I stumbled on a different idea: what if the first thing I heard every morning wasn't a jarring beep, but someone speaking a quote directly to me? Not a notification. Not text on a screen. An actual voice, like someone standing in the room reading Marcus Aurelius or Epictetus to you before your feet hit the floor.

So I set it up. I collected hundreds of motivational quotes — Stoic philosophy, famous speeches, literary passages — and recorded them as voice memos that play as my alarm each morning. Different quote every day, same time. No screens to look at. Just a voice and a message.

Here's what surprised me: it works not because of the quotes themselves, but because of what they do to the first 10 seconds of your day.

A normal alarm triggers fight-or-flight. Your body hears BEEP BEEP BEEP and goes into stress mode. You smash snooze because your brain associates that sound with "threat." But when you wake up to a calm voice saying "The impediment to action advances action — what stands in the way becomes the way," your brain does something different. It processes language. It engages the prefrontal cortex instead of the amygdala. You're thinking before you're reacting.

The compounding effect is real. After about two weeks, I noticed I wasn't dreading mornings anymore. I was actually curious what quote I'd get. Some mornings it's Marcus Aurelius on discipline. Some mornings it's a Bible verse about perseverance. Some mornings it's Churchill telling you to keep going. That micro-moment of curiosity is enough to break the snooze reflex.

I also added a streak system — every morning I get up without snoozing, my streak grows. Snooze once and it resets to zero. Sounds simple, but after building a 14-day streak, the thought of losing it genuinely gets you out of bed. It's the same psychology as Duolingo streaks but for the thing that actually matters — showing up for your day.

The other thing that helped: escalating consequences for snoozing. First snooze, the next quote is a gentle nudge. Second snooze, it gets more pointed. Third snooze, you're getting roasted. "The world is run by those who show up, and you're still horizontal." It sounds funny but it works because it adds social pressure even when you're alone.

Here's the method if you want to try it yourself:

1. Record 5-10 of your favorite quotes as voice memos on your phone
2. Set one as your alarm sound each night before bed (rotate daily)
3. Track your no-snooze streak somewhere visible — a whiteboard, a note on your phone, whatever

The shift from "alarm = threat" to "alarm = message" is what changed everything for me. Mornings went from my worst moment to something I genuinely look forward to.

text:
The Cookie Jar Method

Diogenes of Sinope, an ancient Greek philosopher, used to walk through a brothel every day. He wasn't there to have sex; he was there to build himself. Instead of hiding from temptation (and giving it power over him), he was going to walk right up, look it in the eyes, and refuse. 

  
This is the method that worked for me: the cookie jar method. 

  
Let's say you want to stop eating snacks. Sure, you could avoid buying them. But you're not building any real resistance, just avoiding the problem. The second someone else offers you one, you lose all discipline.

  
Let's say you want to stop being distracted all the time, so you block social media websites. Sure, that can work, but the second they're unblocked you go right back to using them. 

  
When I was younger, I had a problem with eating too many sweets. So, I filled a cookie jar and placed it directly on my desk. When I'd be doing work for 10+ hours a day, that jar would be in the corner of my eye. It was hard ignoring it at first, but eventually I was able to completely build my resistance to cookie-eating. And that was that! 

Remember, if you want to avoid something, make sure that you can refuse it, even if it's available.

I vaped every waking second for ten years cold turkey almost killed me, tapering set me free ( 110 days clean )

I am officially 110 days vape-free, and I need to share exactly how ugly, crazy, and ultimately liberating this process has been.

If you’re researching how to quit right now, you’re probably seeing a lot of posts saying, “Just push through the first three days and you’ll be fine!” I am here to tell you that was absolutely not the case for me.

The Breaking Point

I started vaping when I was 15. For ten solid years, I didn't just vape. I basically was a vape. It was attached to my hand every single second of the day.

I hit my breaking point when the nicotine started giving me crippling, paralyzing anxiety. It got so bad that I would buy a vape, hit it, get a massive panic attack, throw the whole device in the trash out of fear, and then 20 minutes later my brain would scream that I needed a hit. I would literally go buy another one. It was a miserable, exhausting cycle.

Why Cold Turkey Failed Me

At first, I tried going cold turkey and it terrified me. The brain fog was so intense that I felt like I literally couldn't see straight. The shock to my system was too violent and I would always relapse within a few weeks. I also tried 0% vapes, gums, and mints, but nothing stuck.

That’s when I realized I needed to trick my brain. My friend who quit said the method was an app unpuff. I figured I had nothing to lose, so I switched to it and a strict tapering schedule. I slowly lowered my nicotine percentage over a couple of months while extending the time between hits. By the time I finally took my last puff and dropped to absolute zero, my body was somewhat prepared, but my emotions were still a complete wreck.

The Dopamine Crash (and the Crying Phase)

Even with tapering, stepping off that final ledge to zero nicotine is a trip. Here is what my first couple of weeks actually looked like:

Days 1–4 (The Coma)

I went home and basically slept for four days straight. I was so exhausted I would wake up and not even know where I was. Because I was asleep, I honestly thought, "Wow, this isn't that bad!"

Week 2 (The Animal Phase)

Once the sleep wore off, I turned into an absolute emotional monster. I had to warn my family because I was a wreck. I cried every single day for two weeks. I would be mid-workout at Solidcore and just start crying. I would be at dinner with my family, stand up, go to my room, and cry. It sounds pathetic, but honestly it was the best release. Your brain is desperately trying to figure out how to process emotions without a chemical crutch. Let yourself cry.

How I Survived the Cravings

You do not realize how completely messed up your dopamine baseline is until you quit. Because I tapered, the physical shakes were not awful, but the mental cravings were still there. Here is what actually worked to fix my dopamine:

Working out and walking

I forced myself to move every day just to get some natural endorphins.

Freezing cold showers

This was my ultimate cheat code. Whenever I had a craving so bad I thought I was going to lose my mind, I would get in the shower and pull the handle to freezing cold. It literally paralyzed me for a second and completely reset my nervous system. It burns, it sucks, but it absolutely obliterates the craving.

My Takeaway

If you have tried cold turkey and it keeps making you relapse because the withdrawals are too intense, try tapering. Slowly weaning yourself down softens the blow and keeps you from just transferring your addiction to Zyns or nicotine gum. It is still a messy, tear-filled journey, but the brain fog lifts, your dopamine resets, and I promise you will feel completely normal again.

Stay strong, you have got this.

text:
I tracked 100 tasks and discovered why I never finish what I plan

**The problem:** Every day I'd plan to do 5 things. Every night I'd finish 2. Felt like a failure. Repeat.

**The experiment:** For 30 days, I tracked one simple metric for every task:

→ **What I THOUGHT it would take**  
→ **What it ACTUALLY took**

**The results destroyed me:**

📊 **Average estimation accuracy: 52%**

Translation: I was planning *twice as much work* as I could actually do, then wondering why I "lacked discipline."

**Patterns I found (after 100+ tasks):**

**Tasks I underestimated by 50%+:**

* "Quick" emails (thought: 5 min, reality: 15 min)
* Creative work (thought: 1 hour, reality: 2.5 hours)
* Cooking (thought: 20 min, reality: 35 min)
* "Just one more thing" tasks (thought: 10 min, reality: never just 10 min)

**Tasks I overestimated:**

* Boring admin stuff (thought: 30 min, reality: 12 min)
* Returning calls (thought: 20 min, reality: 8 min)

**Time-of-day impact:**

* Morning tasks: 82% accuracy
* Afternoon tasks: 61% accuracy
* Evening tasks: 47% accuracy (I'm basically lying to myself after 6pm)

**What changed:**

Once I *knew* my actual numbers, planning became realistic.

Instead of: ❌ "I'll do 8 hours of work today" (knowing I'll fail)

I started doing: ✅ "I have 6 hours. This creative task will take 2.5 hours based on my data. That admin work will take 45 minutes. That leaves 3 hours for the client project."

**I went from completing 40% of my daily plan to 85%.**

Not because I got more disciplined. Because I stopped lying to myself about how long things take.

**The method (if you want to try):**

1. Before starting ANY task, write down your estimate
2. Time the actual duration
3. Calculate accuracy: (estimated ÷ actual) × 100
4. After 20-30 tasks, look for patterns
5. Adjust your planning based on reality, not fantasy

I built an app to automate this (TimeBoxer - free on iOS, search "TimeBoxer Time Estimator" - it's the orange one!) but you can absolutely do this in a notebook:

    Task              | Est.  | Actual | Accuracy
    Write blog post   | 1h    | 2h 15m | 44%
    Answer emails     | 15m   | 35m    | 43%
    Gym workout       | 45m   | 42m    | 93%

**TL;DR:** Your "discipline problem" might actually be an "estimation problem." Track planned vs. actual time for 30 days. The data will humble you—and then fix you.

Anyone else track this? What were your most shocking discoveries?

If you have ADHD, discipline isn’t about trying harder — it’s about training dopamine

I used to think ADHD made me incapable of discipline.

I’d plan the entire week perfectly…  
Then do nothing.  
I’d make a list of goals…  
Then scroll for 3 hours.  
I’d promise myself to “start early”…  
Then wait for pressure, panic, and deadlines.

It wasn’t because I didn’t care.  
It’s because ADHD rewards urgency, not intention.

That’s when I learned something that changed everything:

>

That means:

* urgent tasks → dopamine
* chaos → dopamine
* last-minute panic → dopamine
* new ideas → dopamine
* YouTube → dopamine
* cleaning your entire room at midnight → dopamine

But sitting down at 4 pm to start your project?  
**Zero stimulation.**  
Your brain doesn’t even see it as a real task.

It’s not that we’re lazy.  
It’s that our dopamine system is wired for “NOW or NEVER.”

So instead of trying to become “normal,”  
I changed my strategy:

# 1. Create artificial urgency

Timers, body double, deadlines you can’t escape.

Not because they’re fun.  
Because they trigger dopamine.

If I tell myself:

>

But if I say:

>

ADHD doesn’t respond to “finish.”  
It responds to “start.”

# 2. Shrink tasks until they feel stupidly easy

ADHD hates “big.”  
It loves “clear.”

* “Clean the room” → fail
* “Throw 3 clothes in the basket” → success
* “Write 1500 words” → fail
* “Type for 5 minutes” → success
* “Work out” → fail
* “Put on shoes + stretch” → success

Tiny actions sound meaningless,  
but they’re dopamine seeds.

# 3. Celebrate completion, not perfection

When you finish something with ADHD,  
even small,  
Your brain releases the “reward chemical.”

That’s how you build consistency.

Not through willpower.  
Through **neurochemical reinforcement.**

Here’s the weirdest part:  
Once I stopped trying to be “motivated all the time,”  
I became more disciplined than ever.

I still struggle.  
But now I understand why.

Discipline for ADHD isn’t about becoming someone else.  
It’s about working with the brain you already have.

**Question for anyone with ADHD:**  
What is ONE task you can shrink into a laughably small version and do TODAY?

I watched my father work himself to death at 15. Here's what it taught me about discipline that nobody wants to hear.

My father collapsed from cardiac arrest right in front of me when I was 15. My whole family watched it happen. He just fell down on a Sunday during a family gathering at our house.

He worked 7 days a week in the epoxy flooring industry. Harsh carcinogenic chemicals. Back-breaking labor. He would stay up until 2-3am at family gatherings on Saturday nights, get maybe 1-2 hours of sleep, then wake up at 4am to grind again. Every single night he came home to the same thing: 12 Corona beers in the mini fridge. That was his only circuit breaker. His only way to turn off the drive that wouldn't stop.

He had no enemies. Not a single one. He uplifted everyone around him. Never talked bad about anyone. Always happy. Pure masculine rock who provided everything for his family.

And discipline killed him.

Two years after he died, I dropped out of high school my junior year. Went up to my mom and told her I wanted to help with bills. I became him. The provider. The grinder.

I built a business to $10k/month by 20 years old. People double my age were calling me a CEO. I worked 15 hours a day. Every single day. For 2 years straight. No social media. No distractions. No substances. Just pure monk mode discipline with daily gym routine. I cut out everything I loved growing up. The things my father bought me to be happy, and sacrificed it all to be "successful."

I thought that's what discipline meant. I thought that's how you honor someone like him.

But here's what nobody tells you about discipline when you have relentless drive:

I plateaued at $2k/month for 8 months. Working my ass off every single day but getting nowhere. I was in autopilot mode. Pattern mode. Mindless execution thinking that's what would propel me forward. The discipline that everyone preaches online, "just do the work", had me stuck.

Then something shifted. I started actually resting. Taking breaks. Thinking instead of just executing. It was hard to do. It was hard to just stop worrying all the time.

But then one night it hit me. The goldmine I'd been sitting on the entire time. Ideas I couldn't see before because I was too busy grinding to actually think diametrically.

I went from $2k to $10k in less than 30 days.

But then the pressure got worse. I couldn't handle it. I'd sacrifice sleep to get campaigns launched. I'd sacrifice entire weekends to get websites done. The voice in my head wouldn't stop telling me to do more. Improve more. Optimize more.

I burned out completely. Just like my father did.

I recently watched Alex Hormozi sit with Tony Robbins and admit he'd been living life like a spreadsheet. Where joy needed to justify its worth. Where love required a return on investment. Where even relaxing demanded productivity metrics.

The advice I followed religiously - "the magic you're looking for is in the work you're avoiding" - that's dangerous advice for people like me. For people who inherited relentless drive from watching their father work until his heart gave out.

For most people that advice means stop procrastinating and do the thing.

But for people with extreme discipline? It becomes justification for never stopping. For never resting. For optimizing everything until you can't even enjoy the things you love anymore.

I'm 21 years old now. And I realized something that would've saved my father's life.

Rest isn't the opposite of discipline. Rest is what makes sustainable discipline possible.

My father didn't have a way to truly rest. He had 12 beers a night to numb out. To turn off the drive that wouldn't stop. And it killed him.

I'm choosing differently. I went back to my roots. Building something I actually love while actually living my life. I'm choosing to be present instead of always calculating the next move.

When I don't truly rest, I go into autopilot mode. Same thing every day. No breakthroughs. Just grinding on fumes until I burn out.

When I actually rest? That's when I see the goldmine. That's when the ideas come. That's when I make the real progress.

If you're reading this and you recognize that drive in yourself... that voice that won't shut off, that constantly tells you to do more, improve more, optimize more, listen to me.

The magic isn't always in the work you're avoiding. Sometimes the magic is in the rest you're denying yourself.

My father worked himself to death because he didn't know that.

I'm choosing differently. And I want to live past 40 to honor him properly.

I made a 13 minute video about this whole story. Not sure if I can drop links here without getting banned, but it's on my profile if you want the full version.

Used to be glued to my phone. My screen time was 6-7 hours. Here is how i fixed it at age 23.

This and last week I used my phone for only 1-2 hours a day.
I feel like I got my brain back. My sleep is finally good, I don't bet anymore. Here is the list of what I changed:

​1. OLauncher
You need this App, I repeat: You 🫵 NEED this APP ASAP!
This Launcher literally changed everything for me. It turns your home screen into a simple text list. No icons, no colors, no red dots. It makes your phone look boring. It completely killed the visual dopamine trigger for me. 

​2. Delete all the Browsers
I deleted my socials long time ago (Instagram, Tiktok, Snapchat) but I ended up scrolling them on Google Chrome web view. It was the same addiction, just a worse interface. Here is what I did:
I deleted the Browsers and now I use Perplexity AI if I wanna look something up on the Internet. It gives me the answer, but it doesn't let me login to social media or surf aimlessly. It's a tool, not a trap.

​3. Grayscale mode
Turn your phone Black & White in the accessibility settings. Combined with OLauncher, your phone looks like a calculator. Even if you find a way to look at content, it’s zero fun without color.

​4. AppBlock (The 9 PM - 1 PM rule)
I set a strict blocking schedule for all distracting apps from 9 PM to 1 PM the next day.

​Night: Forces me to disconnect before bed (better sleep).

​Morning: This is key. I literally can't check my phone when I wake up. I start my day without cheap dopamine and don't get access until after lunch.
​I also use it to lock the Play Store so I can't bypass the block by installing new apps.

​5. Physical Barriers
​Bedroom: Phone charges in another room. I use my Smartwatch alarm to wake up.
​Gym: Phone stays in the locker. I see people texting between sets... don't be that guy. Focus on the lift.

​6. Fill the Void
You can't just stop scrolling and stare at the wall. You need an analog replacement. I started reading books, going for walks, hitting the gym, and started playing Tennis. If you don't fill the time, you will relapse.

​7. Real Life > Trends
I realized I don't need to know every trend or meme. You don't need to know what's happening on TikTok. Real life is so much more beautiful than scrolling through 15-second videos all day. Once you stop caring about "missing out," you actually start living.
